extracted.intended_audience: researchers writing grant proposals for NSF/NIH/foundations and program officers who advise them
extracted.subtask_description: Use the Heilmeier Catechism as a compact, cross-agency framework to evaluate and rewrite a research grant proposal by answering eight core questions concisely and aligning responses to funder review criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: What are you trying to do?
rubrics_metrics.description: State the goal of your project using absolutely no jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate objectives clearly; a child or non-specialist should understand. This becomes your 'elevator pitch.' Answer this in 1–2 sentences before writing and ensure non-experts can grasp it from your text.

rubrics_metrics.name: How is it done today, and what are the limits of current practice?
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the current state of the art and why improvements are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address why improvements are needed and the consequences of doing nothing; describe the state of the art and where current practice is failing. Use this to establish significance and contextualize the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: What's new in your approach, and why do you think it will be successful?
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the novelty of your approach and the evidence supporting its feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain preliminary work and small-scale tests of assumptions; identify the new insight, tool, method, or perspective you bring and why now is the right time. Provide concrete evidence/preliminary data where possible to bolster credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who cares?
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who will benefit and which stakeholders will be affected by the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name specific audiences (researchers, clinicians, public, industry, policymakers). Use this to justify broader impacts and relevance to intended beneficiaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you're successful, what difference will it make?
rubrics_metrics.description: State the concrete impacts, both intellectual and practical, that success will produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer the 'so what' question with concrete changes, long-term significance, and measurable outcomes. Tie to both scholarly contributions and practical/ societal impacts where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: What are the risks, and what is your contingency plan if the initial approach fails?
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify specific technical and managerial/operational risks and mitigation strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List mitigation strategies for each identified risk and describe alternative approaches if Plan A doesn't work. Be honest and specific; reviewers expect realistic risk assessment and contingency planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: How much will it cost?
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the total project cost and justify the budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why requested resources are needed and include cost–benefit considerations. Align budget items with planned activities and milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: How long will it take?
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify project duration, major phases, timing, and critical milestones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a timeline showing major phases and timing; identify mid-term and final 'exams' or checkpoints to assess success. Use milestones to make progress measurable to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with common agency review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Map Heilmeier answers to typical sections of major funders' review criteria (NIH, NSF, ERC, Horizon Europe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mapping to ensure your answers address agency-specific language: e.g., Question 1 → NIH Specific Aims / NSF Project Description; Question 3 → NIH Innovation / NSF Intellectual Merit; Question 4–5 → Broader Impacts/Impact sections. Ensure each Heilmeier response is visible in the corresponding agency section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core proposal quality principles (Why it matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles that the Catechism enforces for strong proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forces clarity (no jargon); demands honesty about risks; requires evidence of preliminary work; anchors review in measurable outcomes; provides a common language across agencies. Use these principles as overarching evaluative lenses when drafting and revising.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use the Catechism
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical steps for applying the eight questions to proposal drafting and review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Answer each question in 1–2 sentences before writing; 2) Review each proposal section against the questions; 3) Use as a self-review before submission; 4) Show to non-expert colleagues—can they answer the questions from your text? These steps are intended to surface gaps and promote concise, clear exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the Catechism doesn't quite fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where the Heilmeier style of evaluation may be less appropriate or needs adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be less applicable for pure exploratory research (unknown outcomes by design), humanities scholarship (metrics may be reductive), policy/social science with diffuse impacts, and long-term basic research with applications decades away. Even in these cases, adopt the spirit—clarity, honest risk assessment, and measurable progress—while adapting specifics.
